attribution.note: Zitron's own calculation in his own post, stated firmly.

semantics.note: Keeps the stipulated $120B demand, the Sightline basis, the later announcements, the 'over 15 times' threshold and the 70–90% share. 'If we assume' sets a premise for the calculation. It is not a hedge.

contract.note: His ratio sets roughly $1.68T of capex against $120B of annual demand. The contract asks for the two to be put on comparable terms, which he never did. That is a reasonable test, but the result depends on a conversion the speaker did not supply. The 70–90% share and the profitability label also need matching evidence.

evidence.note: Sightline's Feb 24, 2026 page confirms the 190GW/777-project input. It gives no demand denominator, no ratio and no customer share.

reviews.rationale: The only item confirms one input, the pipeline size. The packet has no reconciled inventory of later announcements, no comparable capacity-to-demand conversion, no estimate of OpenAI and Anthropic's combined share, and no profitability measure. Nothing establishes or refutes the ratio or the share.

attribution.note: Zitron's own framing sentence in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'vast majority', 'mostly' and his statement that demand exists. The 'cannot afford long-term' clause looks forward but is put as a present judgement. Treating the sentence as an observation is acceptable.

contract.note: Reading 'vast majority' as clear predominance and 'mostly' as more than half is ordinary. Requiring ultimate-workload attribution is fair. Affordability has no stated measure, which leaves that part hard to score.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure of $122B in committed capital (Mar 31, 2026). This bears on its capacity to pay, but committed funding does not show long-term affordability, and it says nothing about demand concentration.
Anthropic's S-1 risk discussion (Oct 26, 2026, before the evaluation date). It describes conditions for continued financing. It is not a finding of inability to pay or a measure of demand share.

reviews.rationale: Neither item gives a market-wide demand denominator, customer shares, or attribution of hyperscaler purchases to OpenAI and Anthropic. The financing evidence is company disclosure and cuts both ways on affordability. The packet does not settle any component.

attribution.note: Zitron's own parenthetical assertion, stated firmly.

semantics.note: The parenthetical 'they aren't' firmly asserts that data centers are unprofitable. Narrowing it to AI data centers matches the section's subject.

contract.note: The plain reading is general net unprofitability after all costs, not every facility. That is ordinary. Using Q1 2026 is an evaluator choice, and the accounting basis is unspecified.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's 10-Q shows a Q1 2026 net loss of $740M and a $3.4B accumulated deficit. This is consistent with the claim, but it is one consolidated operator, not the sector.

Nebius's $621M net income comes mostly from revaluation gains. Its adjusted net loss and its operating costs above revenue point the other way. It is a consolidated, company-reported multi-business result, so it is not decisive.

reviews.rationale: Two neocloud operators' consolidated results point toward losses on an operating basis. They are not representative facility-level or sector-level evidence and do not cover hyperscaler-owned facilities. The packet cannot establish that AI data centers generally were or were not profitable.

attribution.note: Zitron quotes the belief he rejects, then gives his own rebuttal and his own customer list.

semantics.note: Keeps the rejection of universal locked-in demand, the 'I can find' qualifier and the named customer list.

contract.note: Reading 'locked-in' as a disclosed contractual commitment is ordinary. Treating 'I can find' as a claim about the public record is a fair reading of a firm 'the only' statement. Jane Street's deal was widely announced before the post, and he dismissed only VC-dependent firms.

evidence.note: IREN (May 7, 2026) says its planned GPU deployment is not fully contracted, so not all AI capacity is locked in. The same note also shows an NVIDIA contract, which falls outside his list.
In CoreWeave's Apr 15, 2026 announcement, Jane Street, an established trading firm outside his list and not VC-dependent, commits about $6B to AI cloud capacity.

reviews.rationale: The first part holds: e7 shows planned AI deployments that are not fully contracted, so universal locked-in demand is untrue. The customer restriction fails: e8 documents a large committed contract from Jane Street, which is outside his named group and not VC-funded, announced before the post. Both items are company disclosures.
